For a given conductivity cell, the ratio of the separation \(l\) between the two electrodes to the area of cross section \(a\) of an electrode is called the cell constant.

\(\text{Cell constant} = \dfrac{l}{a}\)

Its SI unit is \(\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), conveniently expressed in \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\).

Conductivity \(k\) is the conductance of \(1\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of solution, while molar conductivity \(\Lambda\) is the conductance of the volume \(V\) of solution containing 1 mole of electrolyte. Since \(\Lambda = kV\) and \(V = 1000/c\),

\(\Lambda = \dfrac{1000\,k}{c}\)

where \(c\) is the concentration in \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\).

Unit : \(\Lambda = \dfrac{\mathrm{cm^3\ L^{-1}} \times \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}} = \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) (equivalently \(\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\); the SI unit is \(\mathrm{S\ m^2\ mol^{-1}}\)).

Molten \(\mathrm{KCl}\) contains freely mobile \(\mathrm{K^\oplus}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}\) ions. On applying a potential the anions move to the anode and the cations to the cathode, exactly as the chapter describes for fused \(\mathrm{NaCl}\).

Oxidation at anode :

\(2\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

Reduction at cathode :

\(\mathrm{K^\oplus}(l) + \mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K}(l)\)

Net cell reaction :

\(2\mathrm{K^\oplus}(l) + 2\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}(l) \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{K}(l) + \mathrm{Cl_2(g)}\)

Molten potassium is formed at the cathode (the negative electrode) and pale green chlorine gas is released at the anode (the positive electrode).

Any two of the three functions the chapter lists :

i. It provides an electrical contact between the two solutions and thereby completes the electrical circuit.

ii. It prevents mixing of the two solutions.

iii. It maintains electrical neutrality in both the solutions by transfer of ions.

In the given reaction \(\mathrm{Al}\) is oxidised, so the \(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}}\,|\,\mathrm{Al}\) electrode is the anode, and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced, so the \(\mathrm{Ni^{2\oplus}}\,|\,\mathrm{Ni}\) electrode is the cathode.

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0(\text{cathode}) - E^0(\text{anode}) = E^0_{Ni} - E^0_{Al}\)

\(= -0.25\ \mathrm{V} - (-1.66\ \mathrm{V}) = 1.41\ \mathrm{V}\)

Note that the coefficients 2 and 3 do not enter the calculation : \(E^0_{cell}\) is an intensive property and does not change when a half reaction is multiplied by a numerical factor.

For a general reaction \(a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \longrightarrow c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}\), the Nernst equation gives the cell voltage as

\(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{2.303\,RT}{n\mathrm{F}}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b}\)

and at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\), since \(2.303\,RT/\mathrm{F} = 0.0592\ \mathrm{V}\),

\(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{n}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b}\)

The FIRST term, \(E^0_{cell}\), represents standard state electrochemical conditions. The SECOND term, \(-\dfrac{0.0592}{n}\log_{10}Q\), is the correction factor for non-standard state conditions; it vanishes when all concentrations are 1 M, and then \(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell}\).

The cell potential is called the standard cell potential when it is measured under standard state conditions, namely :

- concentration of every solution 1 M,
- pressure of every gas 1 atm,
- solids and liquids in their pure form,
- temperature \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Under these conditions the correction term of the Nernst equation is zero and \(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell}\).

The reaction in which electrons are consumed is a reduction and so occurs at the cathode; the one in which electrons are released is an oxidation and so occurs at the anode.

\(\mathrm{Au^{3\oplus}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Au(s)}\)  — cathode (+)

\(\mathrm{Mg(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)  — anode (\(-\))

By convention the anode is written at the extreme left and the cathode at the extreme right, a single vertical line marks a phase boundary and a double vertical line the salt bridge. Hence the cell is

\(\mathrm{Mg(s)}\,|\,\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,||\,\mathrm{Au^{3\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Au(s)}\)

One mole of electrons carries a charge of \(96500\ \mathrm{C}\) (one faraday). Hence

moles of electrons \(= \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{C}}{96500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}} = 1.036 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}\)

number of electrons \(= 1.036 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 6.24 \times 10^{18}\) electrons

A SINGLE vertical line between two phases indicates the phase boundary, that is, direct contact between those two phases (for example between the metal electrode and the solution of its ions).

A DOUBLE vertical line between the two solutions indicates that they are connected by a salt bridge.

On dilution the conductivity DECREASES.

Conductivity is the electrical conductance of unit volume \((1\ \mathrm{cm^3})\) of solution, so it depends on the number of current-carrying ions present in unit volume.

On dilution the TOTAL number of ions does increase, because the degree of dissociation increases. But this increase is not in proportion to the dilution. Therefore the number of ions per unit volume of solution decreases, and with it the conductivity.

The chapter's own illustration : \(100\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of a solution containing \(8 \times 10^{20}\) ions has \(8 \times 10^{18}\) ions per \(\mathrm{cm^3}\). On dilution to \(1000\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) the number of ions rises only to \(64 \times 10^{20}\), that is \(6.8 \times 10^{18}\) per \(\mathrm{cm^3}\) — fewer than before.

A salt bridge is a U tube containing a saturated solution of an inert electrolyte such as \(\mathrm{KCl}\) or \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}\) together with 5 % agar solution, which sets into a gel so that it does not run out when the tube is inverted. Its two ends are closed with glass wool plugs and dipped one into each half cell solution of a galvanic cell.

The electrolyte is chosen so that its ions do not react with the ions of the electrode solutions or with the electrodes. The salt bridge completes the electrical circuit between the two half cells while keeping the two solutions from mixing.

Reduction at cathode : two reductions compete — that of \(\mathrm{Na^\oplus}\) \((E^0 = -2.71\ \mathrm{V})\) and that of water \((E^0 = -0.83\ \mathrm{V})\). Water has the higher standard potential and therefore the greater tendency to be reduced, so the cathode reaction is

\(2\mathrm{H_2O}(l) + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)}\)

Oxidation at anode : oxidation of \(\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}\) competes with oxidation of water. On standard potentials alone water should be oxidised, but experiment shows that the gas released is \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\), not \(\mathrm{O_2}\) — the reason being overvoltage. Hence

\(2\mathrm{Cl^\ominus(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

Overall cell reaction :

\(2\mathrm{Cl^\ominus(aq)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)}\)

Because \(\mathrm{Na^\oplus}\) ions remain unreacted while \(\mathrm{OH^\ominus}\) ions are formed, the \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) solution is converted to \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution.

Quantity of electricity passed :

\(Q = I \times t = 0.8\ \mathrm{A} \times 1 \times 60 \times 60\ \mathrm{s} = 2880\ \mathrm{C}\)

Moles of electrons passed :

\(= \dfrac{Q}{96500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}} = \dfrac{2880}{96500} = 0.0298\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}\)

The answer does not depend on the electrolyte being \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) — the charge passed fixes the moles of electrons whatever is being electrolysed. (Those \(0.0298\) mol of electrons would deposit \(0.0149\) mol of \(\mathrm{Ca}\), since \(\mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ca}\).)

While constructing a galvanic cell the electrode with the HIGHER standard potential is the cathode and that with the lower standard potential is the anode. Here \(E^0_{Co} = 1.82\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(E^0_{Mn} = -1.18\ \mathrm{V}\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}}\,|\,\mathrm{Co}\) is the cathode and \(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}}\,|\,\mathrm{Mn}\) the anode.

Cell formula (anode on the left) :

\(\mathrm{Mn(s)}\,|\,\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,||\,\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Co(s)}\)

Electrode reactions :

anode  \(\mathrm{Mn(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

cathode  \(\mathrm{Co^{3\oplus}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Co(s)}\)

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0(\text{cathode}) - E^0(\text{anode}) = 1.82\ \mathrm{V} - (-1.18\ \mathrm{V}) = 3.00\ \mathrm{V}\)

From \(\Delta G^0 = -n\mathrm{F}E^0_{cell}\),

\(E^0_{cell} = -\dfrac{\Delta G^0}{n\mathrm{F}}\)

\(\Delta G^0\) is an EXTENSIVE property : its value depends on the amount of substance. Suppose the stoichiometric equation of the redox reaction is multiplied by 2, so that the amounts oxidised and reduced are doubled. Then \(\Delta G^0\) doubles to \(2\Delta G^0\) — but the moles of electrons transferred also double, from \(n\) to \(2n\). Therefore

\(E^0_{cell} = -\dfrac{2\Delta G^0}{2n\mathrm{F}} = -\dfrac{\Delta G^0}{n\mathrm{F}}\)

which is the value before doubling. \(E^0_{cell}\) is thus unchanged by multiplying the reaction, that is, it is independent of the amount of substance — an INTENSIVE property. The two extensive quantities \(\Delta G^0\) and \(n\) scale together and their ratio does not.

[Textbook misprint: the printed numbering of Exercise question 3 runs i, ii, iii, iv, v, vi, viii, ix, x, xi — the label vii is skipped. No question is missing; the block has ten items and the labels above are transcribed exactly as printed.]

Two relations are combined.

i. From electrochemistry, the standard Gibbs energy change of the cell reaction and the standard cell potential are related by

\(\Delta G^0 = -n\mathrm{F}E^0_{cell}\)

ii. From thermodynamics, the standard Gibbs energy change of a chemical reaction and its equilibrium constant are related by

\(\Delta G^0 = -RT\ln K\)

Equating the two expressions for \(\Delta G^0\),

\(-n\mathrm{F}E^0_{cell} = -RT\ln K\)

\(E^0_{cell} = \dfrac{RT}{n\mathrm{F}}\ln K = \dfrac{2.303\,RT}{n\mathrm{F}}\log_{10}K\)

At \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\), \(2.303\,RT/\mathrm{F} = 0.0592\ \mathrm{V}\), so

\(E^0_{cell} = \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{n}\log_{10}K\)

which is the required relationship.

Every oxidation must be accompanied by a reduction; the occurrence of only oxidation or only reduction is not possible. A single electrode carries only one half reaction, so no measurable current can be drawn from it in isolation and its potential cannot be measured on its own.

To measure a potential, two electrodes must be combined so that a complete redox reaction occurs. What is then measured is the CELL potential, which is the algebraic sum of the two electrode potentials — not the potential of either electrode alone.

The way round this is to choose an arbitrary standard electrode as a reference point. Chemists have chosen the standard hydrogen electrode (\(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas at 1 atm in contact with 1 M \(\mathrm{H^\oplus}\)) and assigned its potential the value zero. When one electrode of the cell has zero potential, the measured cell potential equals the potential of the other electrode. So electrode potentials are always RELATIVE values measured against a reference, never absolute measurements of a single electrode.

The net cell reaction of the lead accumulator during discharge is

\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

As the cell operates to generate current, \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) is CONSUMED, so its concentration (and hence the density of the electrolyte) decreases. The cell potential depends on the sulphuric acid concentration, so it falls with it.

The potential is raised again by RECHARGING. When it has fallen to about 1.8 V, an external potential slightly greater than 2 V is applied across the electrodes. The cell then works as an electrolytic cell, the electrode reactions reverse, and the net reaction becomes

\(2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)}\)

\(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) is regenerated, its concentration (density) rises, and in turn the cell potential increases.

In the nickel-cadmium (NICAD) storage cell the anode is cadmium metal, the cathode is nickel (IV) oxide, \(\mathrm{NiO_2}\), supported on \(\mathrm{Ni}\), and the electrolyte solution is basic.

Anodic oxidation :

\(\mathrm{Cd(s)} + 2\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cd(OH)_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

Cathodic reduction :

\(\mathrm{NiO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l) + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ni(OH)_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)}\)

Overall cell reaction :

\(\mathrm{Cd(s)} + \mathrm{NiO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cd(OH)_2(s)} + \mathrm{Ni(OH)_2(s)}\)

The product at each electrode is a solid that adheres to the electrode surface, which is why the cell can be recharged. Its potential is about 1.4 V.

**Statement of the law.** At infinite dilution each ion migrates independent of the co-ion and contributes to the total molar conductivity of an electrolyte irrespective of the nature of the other ion with which it is associated. Hence the molar conductivity at zero concentration is the sum of the contributions of the cation and the anion :

\(\Lambda_0 = n^\oplus \lambda^0_\oplus + n^\ominus \lambda^0_\ominus\)

where \(\lambda^0_\oplus\) and \(\lambda^0_\ominus\) are the molar ionic conductivities and \(n^\oplus\), \(n^\ominus\) the numbers of moles of cation and anion in the formula of the electrolyte.

**Why it is needed for a weak electrolyte.** For a STRONG electrolyte \(\Lambda\) varies linearly with \(\sqrt{c}\), so \(\Lambda_0\) can be found by extrapolating the \(\Lambda\) versus \(\sqrt{c}\) plot to zero concentration. For a WEAK electrolyte that plot does not approach linearity, so extrapolation fails. Kohlrausch law lets \(\Lambda_0\) of the weak electrolyte be assembled from the \(\Lambda_0\) values of strong electrolytes, which CAN be obtained by extrapolation.

**Example — acetic acid.**

\(\Lambda_0(\mathrm{HCl}) + \Lambda_0(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}) - \Lambda_0(\mathrm{NaCl})\)

\(= (\lambda^0_{\mathrm{H^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}}) + (\lambda^0_{\mathrm{Na^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{CH_3COO^\ominus}}) - (\lambda^0_{\mathrm{Na^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}})\)

\(= \lambda^0_{\mathrm{H^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{CH_3COO^\ominus}} = \Lambda_0(\mathrm{CH_3COOH})\)

All three electrolytes on the left are strong, so each \(\Lambda_0\) is available by extrapolation and \(\Lambda_0\) of the weak acid follows.

**Construction.** The electrolytic cell is a container holding fused \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), in which two graphite electrodes are immersed. They are joined by metallic wires to a battery (a source of direct current). The electrode connected to the positive terminal of the battery is the anode and that connected to the negative terminal is the cathode.

**What happens.** Fused \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) contains freely mobile \(\mathrm{Na^\oplus}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}\) ions. On applying the potential, the cathode attracts \(\mathrm{Na^\oplus}\) and the anode attracts \(\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}\); since these are charged particles their migration constitutes the electric current. At the electrodes they are discharged.

Oxidation at anode :

\(2\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

(each \(\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}\) first gives one electron to the anode to form a neutral \(\mathrm{Cl}\) atom — the primary process — and two \(\mathrm{Cl}\) atoms then combine to \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) — the secondary process)

Reduction at cathode :

\(2\mathrm{Na^\oplus}(l) + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Na}(l)\)

Overall cell reaction :

\(2\mathrm{Na^\oplus}(l) + 2\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}(l) \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Na}(l) + \mathrm{Cl_2(g)}\)

**Results.** A pale green \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) gas is released at the anode and molten silvery-white sodium is formed at the cathode. The decomposition of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) into \(\mathrm{Na}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) is nonspontaneous; the electrical energy supplied by the battery forces it to occur.

Stoichiometry at the cathode :

\(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\), so mole ratio \(= \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}}\)

Mass of product :

\(W = \dfrac{I\,(\mathrm{A}) \times t\,(\mathrm{s})}{96500\ (\mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus})} \times \text{mole ratio} \times \text{molar mass}\)

\(2.4\ \mathrm{g} = \dfrac{I \times 3600\ \mathrm{s}}{96500} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 63.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(I = \dfrac{2.4 \times 2 \times 96500}{63.5 \times 3600} = \dfrac{463200}{228600} = 2.03\ \mathrm{A}\)

A current of about 2.03 ampere is required.

The reaction \(2\mathrm{Cu^\oplus(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\) is a disproportionation, made of

oxidation  \(\mathrm{Cu^\oplus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}} + \mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

reduction  \(\mathrm{Cu^\oplus} + \mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\)

so ONE mole of electrons is transferred, \(n = 1\).

Using \(E^0_{cell} = \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{n}\log_{10}K\),

\(E^0_{cell} = \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{1} \times \log_{10}(1.2 \times 10^{6})\)

\(= 0.0592\ \mathrm{V} \times 6.0792 = 0.36\ \mathrm{V}\)

The standard potential of the cell is 0.36 V. (It is positive, as it must be, because \(K \gg 1\) means the reaction is spontaneous.)

Anode (left) is the \(\mathrm{Zn}\) electrode, cathode (right) the hydrogen electrode :

\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)  (oxidation)

\(2\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2(g)}\)  (reduction)

\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\), \(n = 2\)

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0(\text{cathode}) - E^0(\text{anode}) = 0 - (-0.76\ \mathrm{V}) = 0.76\ \mathrm{V}\)

Because \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is a gas its concentration term is replaced by its partial pressure :

\(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}]\,P_{\mathrm{H_2}}}{[\mathrm{H^\oplus}]^2}\)

\(= 0.76\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0296\ \mathrm{V} \times \log_{10}\dfrac{0.2 \times 1.8}{(1.6)^2}\)

\(= 0.76\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0296\ \mathrm{V} \times \log_{10}(0.1406)\)

\(= 0.76\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0296\ \mathrm{V} \times (-0.8516) = 0.76\ \mathrm{V} + 0.0252\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(= 0.785\ \mathrm{V}\)

(\(E^0_{Zn} = -0.76\ \mathrm{V}\) is taken from Table 5.1 of the chapter.)

Anode (left) is \(\mathrm{Zn}\), cathode (right) is \(\mathrm{Cr}\). Balancing the electrons, 3 and 2 respectively, gives \(n = 6\) :

\(3\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}(aq)} \longrightarrow 3\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Cr(s)}\)

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{Cr} - E^0_{Zn} = -0.74\ \mathrm{V} - (-0.76\ \mathrm{V}) = 0.02\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{6}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}]^3}{[\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}}]^2}\)

\(= 0.02\ \mathrm{V} - \dfrac{0.0592}{6}\ \mathrm{V} \times \log_{10}\dfrac{(0.08)^3}{(0.1)^2}\)

\(= 0.02\ \mathrm{V} - 0.009867\ \mathrm{V} \times \log_{10}(0.0512)\)

\(= 0.02\ \mathrm{V} - 0.009867\ \mathrm{V} \times (-1.2907) = 0.02\ \mathrm{V} + 0.0127\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(= 0.0327\ \mathrm{V}\)

**What it is.** For a given conductivity cell the ratio of the separation \(l\) between the two electrodes to the area of cross section \(a\) of an electrode is the cell constant :

\(\text{Cell constant} = \dfrac{l}{a}\)

It appears in the working form of the conductivity relation, \(k = \dfrac{\text{cell constant}}{R}\).

**Units.** The SI unit is \(\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), conveniently expressed in \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\).

**How it is determined experimentally.** \(l\) and \(a\) cannot be measured accurately for a real cell, so the constant is obtained from a solution of KNOWN conductivity — 1 M, 0.1 M or 0.01 M \(\mathrm{KCl}\), whose conductivity is well tabulated at various temperatures.

The conductivity cell containing the \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution is placed in one arm of a Wheatstone bridge with a known variable resistance \(R_x\) in the other; A.C. is used and a current detector D shows the null point. The sliding contact F is moved along the uniform wire AB until the detector shows no deflection, at C. Then

\(R_{solution} = \dfrac{l(\mathrm{AC})}{l(\mathrm{BC})} \times R_x\)

and since \(k_{\mathrm{KCl}}\) is known,

\(\text{Cell constant} = k_{\mathrm{KCl}} \times R_{solution}\)

**i. Quantity of electricity passed.** Measure the current \(I\) and note the time \(t\) for which it is passed :

\(Q\,(\mathrm{C}) = I\,(\mathrm{A}) \times t\,(\mathrm{s})\)

**ii. Moles of electrons passed.** The charge of one mole of electrons is 96500 C (one faraday), so

\(\text{moles of electrons} = \dfrac{Q\,(\mathrm{C})}{96500\ (\mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus})}\)

**iii. Moles of product formed.** Write the balanced half reaction at the electrode. Its stoichiometry gives

\(\text{mole ratio} = \dfrac{\text{moles of product formed in the half reaction}}{\text{moles of electrons required in the half reaction}}\)

For example \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\) gives a mole ratio of \(1/2\). Then

\(\text{moles of product} = \dfrac{I \times t}{96500} \times \text{mole ratio}\)

**iv. Mass of product.**

\(W = \text{moles of product} \times \text{molar mass} = \dfrac{I\,(\mathrm{A}) \times t\,(\mathrm{s})}{96500\ (\mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus})} \times \text{mole ratio} \times \text{molar mass of product}\)

**During discharge** the anode (\(-\)) is the spongy lead plate and the cathode (+) is the plate bearing \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\).

Oxidation at anode :

\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

(spongy lead is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Pb^{2\oplus}}\), which then combines with \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) from \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) to precipitate insoluble \(\mathrm{PbSO_4}\))

Reduction at cathode :

\(\mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 4\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

Net cell reaction :

\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

**During recharging** the cell functions as an electrolytic cell and the two electrodes are INTERCHANGED : the \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\) electrode becomes the anode (+) and the lead electrode the cathode (\(-\)). Each reaction is the reverse of the corresponding discharge reaction.

Oxidation at anode (+) :

\(\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 4\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

Reduction at cathode (\(-\)) :

\(\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)}\)

Net reaction on recharging :

\(2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)}\)

**Electrodes.** Both anode and cathode are porous carbon rods containing a small amount of finely divided platinum metal, which acts as a catalyst. Hydrogen gas is bubbled continuously through the anode (\(-\)) and oxygen gas through the cathode (+).

**Electrolyte.** Hot aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\) solution.

**Oxidation at anode (\(-\)) :** hydrogen gas is oxidised to water.

\(2\mathrm{H_2(g)} + 4\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{H_2O}(l) + 4\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

**Reduction at cathode (+) :** \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{OH^\ominus}\).

\(\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} + 4\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)}\)

**Net cell reaction :**

\(2\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

The overall cell reaction is simply the combustion of hydrogen to liquid water, although the fuel and the oxidant never react directly. The cell potential is

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{cathode} - E^0_{anode} = 0.4\ \mathrm{V} - (-0.83\ \mathrm{V}) = 1.23\ \mathrm{V}\)

**Anode (\(-\)) :** the zinc container of the cell, lined inside with a porous paper.

**Cathode (+) :** an inert graphite rod at the centre of the cell, surrounded by a paste of manganese dioxide \((\mathrm{MnO_2})\) and carbon black. The electrolyte is a moist paste of \(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{ZnCl_2}\) thickened with starch.

**Oxidation at anode :** metallic zinc is oxidised to zinc ions.

\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

**Reduction at cathode :** \(\mathrm{NH_4^\oplus}\) ions are reduced,

\(2\mathrm{NH_4^\oplus(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\)

and the hydrogen so produced is at once oxidised by \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\), which prevents it collecting on the cathode,

\(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{MnO_2(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn_2O_3(s)} + \mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

so that the net cathode reaction is

\(2\mathrm{NH_4^\oplus(aq)} + 2\mathrm{MnO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn_2O_3(s)} + 2\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

**Overall cell reaction :**

\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\mathrm{NH_4^\oplus(aq)} + 2\mathrm{MnO_2(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{Mn_2O_3(s)} + 2\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

The ammonia produced combines with \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\) to form a soluble complex ion :

\(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 4\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} \longrightarrow [\mathrm{Zn(NH_3)_4}]^{2\oplus}\mathrm{(aq)}\)

In the electrochemical series the half reactions are written as REDUCTIONS, so the species on the LEFT side are the oxidising agents. A free metal or a non-metal anion appears on the right side and is a reducing agent, not an oxidising agent. Oxidising strength increases with increasing \(E^0\).

Of the seven species listed, three are NOT oxidising agents : \(\mathrm{Al}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe}\) are free metals and \(\mathrm{Br^\ominus}\) is an anion — all three are right-side species, hence reducing agents.

The oxidising agents are \(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{I_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\). Arranged in order of INCREASING strength, that is increasing \(E^0\) :

\(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}}\,(-1.66\ \mathrm{V}) < \mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}}\,(-0.4\ \mathrm{V}) < \mathrm{I_2}\,(0.54\ \mathrm{V}) < \mathrm{Cl_2}\,(1.36\ \mathrm{V})\)

So \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) is the strongest and \(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}}\) the weakest oxidising agent of the four.

In the electrochemical series the half reactions are written as reductions, so the species on the RIGHT side are the reducing agents, and reducing strength increases as \(E^0\) becomes more negative.

\(\mathrm{Br_2}\,(1.09\ \mathrm{V})\) and \(\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}\,(0.8\ \mathrm{V})\) are the LEFT-side species of their half reactions \(\big(\mathrm{Br_2} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Br^\ominus}\) and \(\mathrm{Ag^\oplus} + \mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}\big)\), so they are oxidising agents and are excluded.

The remaining five are reducing agents : \(\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) are free metals; \(\mathrm{Ni}\) is a free metal; and \(\mathrm{Ti^{2\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ce^{3\oplus}}\) are the REDUCED members of higher couples — the quoted values \(-0.37\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(1.61\ \mathrm{V}\) belong to \(\mathrm{Ti^{3\oplus}}/\mathrm{Ti^{2\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ce^{4\oplus}}/\mathrm{Ce^{3\oplus}}\), and Table 5.1 of the chapter itself lists \(\mathrm{Ce^{4\oplus}},\ \mathrm{Ce^{3\oplus}}\,|\,\mathrm{Pt}\) at \(+1.610\ \mathrm{V}\). Both are therefore right-side species, though very weak reducing agents.

In order of INCREASING reducing strength, that is decreasing \(E^0\) :

\(\mathrm{Ce^{3\oplus}}\,(1.61\ \mathrm{V}) < \mathrm{Ni}\,(-0.23\ \mathrm{V}) < \mathrm{Ti^{2\oplus}}\,(-0.37\ \mathrm{V}) < \mathrm{Mg}\,(-2.36\ \mathrm{V}) < \mathrm{K}\,(-2.93\ \mathrm{V})\)

So \(\mathrm{K}\) is the strongest reducing agent of the set.

[Note : the chapter's *Remember* box says the right side of a half reaction carries "free metals or anions of non metals", which would exclude the two cations \(\mathrm{Ti^{2\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Ce^{3\oplus}}\). That box is a simplification — Table 5.1 itself contains couples such as \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}}/\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}/\mathrm{Cu^\oplus}\) and \(\mathrm{Ce^{4\oplus}}/\mathrm{Ce^{3\oplus}}\) whose right-side species IS a cation, and the potentials this question supplies are exactly those couples' potentials.]

A cell reaction is spontaneous under standard state conditions only if \(E^0_{cell}\) is positive, where \(E^0_{cell} = E^0(\text{species reduced}) - E^0(\text{species oxidised})\).

**a.** \(\mathrm{Ca}\) is oxidised, \(\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced.

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}/Cd}} - E^0_{\mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}/Ca}} = -0.403\ \mathrm{V} - (-2.866\ \mathrm{V}) = +2.463\ \mathrm{V}\)

Positive, so the reaction WOULD occur spontaneously.

**b.** \(\mathrm{Br^\ominus}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Br_2}\), \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced.

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}/Sn}} - E^0_{\mathrm{Br_2/Br^\ominus}} = -0.136\ \mathrm{V} - 1.080\ \mathrm{V} = -1.216\ \mathrm{V}\)

Negative, so the reaction would NOT occur spontaneously. (The reverse reaction, \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) oxidising \(\mathrm{Sn}\), is the spontaneous one.)

**c.** \(\mathrm{Ag}\) is oxidised, \(\mathrm{Ni^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced.

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{\mathrm{Ni^{2\oplus}/Ni}} - E^0_{\mathrm{Ag^\oplus/Ag}} = -0.257\ \mathrm{V} - 0.799\ \mathrm{V} = -1.056\ \mathrm{V}\)

Negative, so the reaction would NOT occur spontaneously.

Only reaction (a) is spontaneous under standard state conditions.
